key_concept: PCR repeats three steps (denaturation, annealing, extension), and primers attach to complementary sequences on single-stranded template DNA during annealing.
steps: Recall the three steps of each PCR cycle in order: denaturation, then annealing, then extension.
Denaturation (about $94$–$96^\circ C$): high temperature breaks the hydrogen bonds, separating double-stranded DNA into two single strands. No primer binding happens here.

Annealing (about $50$–$65^\circ C$): the temperature is lowered so the short synthetic oligonucleotide primers can hydrogen-bond (hybridise) to their complementary sequences flanking the target region on each single strand.
Extension (about $72^\circ C$): thermostable Taq DNA polymerase adds nucleotides to the $3'$ end of each bound primer, synthesising the new strand.
Primers bind in the annealing step, so the answer is option (3), which matches the official key.
why_not_others: Denaturation only separates the strands and extension only lengthens primers that are already bound. Ligation is not a PCR step at all; it is the joining of DNA fragments by DNA ligase in recombinant DNA work.
common_trap: Choosing extension because primers are 'used' there, or ligation because the word sounds like joining, when the actual binding (hybridisation) of primers happens during annealing.
time_saving_tip: Memorise the order 'D-A-E' (Denature, Anneal, Extend): strands separate, primers stick, polymerase extends. Ligation can be eliminated at once because it is not a PCR step.
